sentences.text: Task 2. Keaton is interviewing TY Chow for Hidden Hong Kong Tours YouTube channel.
TY is the owner of a porcelain factory in Hong Kong.
Listen to the interview and complete the information in the spaces below.
The first one has been provided as an example.
You now have 30 seconds to study the task.
At the end of the task, you will have one minute to tidy up your answers.
Thanks for meeting me today T .Y.
So why don’t you tell me a bit about your factory to get us started?
Well, as you might already know, my factory’s name is Guang China Works, We were the first, and are now the last, hand -painted porcelain factory in Hong Kong.
Believe it or not, we have been open since 1928.
Was there anything about your porcelain which stood out from the rest?
Well, that’s a good question.
I think one thing was that we weren't following traditional styles of porcelain painting.
painting. We were known for using gold, pink, yellow, sky blue, and turquoise.
Those sorts of colours.
Not traditional at all.
And our unique painting techniques were famous in the city as well.
What do you mean by unique painting techniques?
Yes, well, most factories at that time were using plain designs on porcelain for everyday day use.
Our approach made our porcelain more expensive.
So, it was not for everyone.
But if you were the pioneer in your field and well -known and appreciated, how did things change so drastically?
That's a long story.
I remember my father telling me back in the day when my grandmother Some other first started the business in the 1920s, she hired over 30 painters.
Over 30 painters?
Business must have been booming then!
The demand was so high we expanded our business around Hong Kong during the 70s.
We ended up opening six branches.
But unfortunately that didn’t last long.
After around 20 years, in the 1990s, we had to downsize because of the economic downturn.
People were facing many difficulties financially and many businesses left.
That’s sad. I suppose it must have left you feeling so helpless.
Well, not as helpless as we’re feeling right now.
Well, Seeing the current situation, we’re facing possible shutdown.
Yes, I’d heard that and I was wondering if you could explain why.
How come the porcelain factories continued to struggle and to lose money?
Well, there are a number of reasons.
The first one is that the factories moved to Mainland China.
Was that because the economy or talent was better in Mainland China compared to Hong Kong?
No, it was because of the lower wages and rent.
Because the wages and rent were lower, business was more profitable.
And that meant it became more and more attractive to move your factory to Mainland China.
You said there were other reasons as well, right?
many factories can’t recover.
Why are there no more young workers then?
That’s a good question.
I think the skills are difficult to learn.
OK, so how have you continued to survive despite the downturn?
Well, fortunately, we still had two groups of customers who kept us in business in the 1990s.
One of them was five -star hotels.
Five -star hotels were still ordering from us because they often displayed porcelain in hotel lobbies.
You know, for decoration.
That makes sense.
But did that mean that there were no individual customers making purchases then?
Well there were quite a few actually.
really, There were many who loved our products and wanted a piece of history and their culture in their homes.
But most of these people were overseas, so we had a lot of overseas customers.
OK. So, what are the most popular patterns among customers nowadays since you have quite a variety of them?
Well, you often see patterns with flowers on porcelain in local markets.
where they aren’t as popular as you might think.
It’s images of Chinese mythology that are really popular with customers.
I think they like having these magical creatures on their pieces because they are such a big part part of the Chinese culture I suppose.
So, do customers request to have people painted on their porcelain as well?
Like Emperors from the past, or other important historical figures, that sort of thing?
Or maybe images or of landscapes?
Actually, they tend to prefer something a bit more personal.
A lot of customers overseas, These, especially from the UK, will ask for their family emblems to be included in the designs so they can pass it down to their children.
OK, well, thank you.
This has been wonderful.
Thank you so much for this interview T .Y.
